question: ATS 7.10.1.D.2 on current transformers requires polarity results to:
choices: Be within 2% of the adjacent phase
Agree with the transformer markings
Be ignored if the ratio is within 5%
Match the relay time dial
explanation: Polarity agrees with the marks. A ratio can look plausible while H1/X1 are reversed, and a reversed CT in a differential scheme looks like an internal fault as soon as load flows.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.D.2

question: How many grounding points does ATS 7.10.1 allow on a CT secondary circuit?
choices: None; secondaries must float
Exactly one, at the location the drawings specify
One at each end of the run
One per phase plus one on the neutral
explanation: The secondary circuit is grounded, and it has only one grounding point, located where the engineer showed it, consistent with IEEE C57.13.3. A second ground circulates current. No ground lets the circuit float.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.9 and D.9; ref. IEEE C57.13.3-2014, 5.3 (ground at only one point)

question: ATS 7.10.2.D.3 ratio-error limits for voltage transformers are:
choices: ±0.1% for revenue metering; the other-applications sentence states +1.2% ratio and ±17.5 mrad phase angle
±3% for every VT, revenue included
±0.5%, the power-transformer TTR rule
No numeric limit; only polarity is checked
explanation: Revenue metering is ±0.1% ratio and ±0.9 mrad. Other applications are written as not exceeding +1.2% ratio and ±17.5 mrad (one degree). A ±3% field screen from a VT manufacturer bulletin is a different test, done at very low voltage, and is not this paragraph.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.2.D.3

question: Insulation resistance of a current transformer and its secondary wiring, ATS 7.10.1, is:
choices: 5000 V DC for 10 minutes
1000 V DC for one minute, unless solid-state parts cannot take it
Table 100.19 AC withstand
A megger is forbidden on CT wiring
explanation: 7.10.1.B.1 specifies 1000 V DC for one minute on each CT and its secondary wiring to ground. If a device on that wiring cannot survive the voltage, follow the manufacturer instead of forcing the shot.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.1

question: ATS 7.10.1 requires an excitation test on which CTs?
choices: Only metering CTs below 600 V
CTs used for relaying
Every window CT, and never a bushing CT
None; excitation was removed from the section
explanation: ATS 7.10.1.B.4 calls for an excitation test on relaying current transformers, done in accordance with IEEE C57.13.1. Clause 6.5 of that guide says the test checks the accuracy rating and looks for shorted turns, against the manufacturer’s curve. Metering CTs still get ratio and polarity.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.4 and D.4; ref. IEEE C57.13.1-2017, clause 6.5

question: Burden of a CT circuit is measured:
choices: At the shorting block, with the secondary open under load
At the CT shorting terminal block, per IEEE C57.13.1
Only on the primary bushing
With a megohmmeter
explanation: ATS 7.10.1.B.5 measures the current-circuit burden at the CT shorting block, in accordance with IEEE C57.13.1. Clause 6.7 says that check is made with secondary current flowing, preferably near rated current, into a known burden. Extra lead and extra relays are what push the CT toward saturation.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.5; ref. IEEE C57.13.1-2017, clause 6.7

question: Ratio of a CT, ATS 7.10.1, is verified by:
choices: The voltage or current method in IEEE C57.13.1
A megohmmeter only
Primary injection at 300% for Table 100.7
Tan delta of the secondary
explanation: ATS 7.10.1.B.3 names the voltage method or the current method, both under IEEE C57.13.1. Those methods are in clause 8. Polarity, clause 9, still has to agree with the marks. A ratio that matches the nameplate with the marks reversed is a failed polarity test.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.3 and D.2; ref. IEEE C57.13.1-2017, clauses 8 and 9

question: You finished a CT with a DC resistance reading and skipped excitation. The core is:
choices: Demagnetized, because DC resistance is gentle
Likely left magnetized; excitation is what works the flux back down
Unaffected by DC
Required to be hipot tested next
explanation: A DC resistance reading can leave the core magnetized. To demagnetize it, use the excitation hookup, raise the AC voltage past saturation, and then lower that voltage slowly and continuously all the way to zero. Reaching saturation and stopping there does not take the magnetism out. ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.4 still requires the excitation test on relaying CTs.

question: IEEE 30°, IEEE 45°, and the 10/50 knee are:
choices: Three names for one voltage
Different markers on the excitation curve
Ratio-error classes
Burden ratings in ohms
explanation: The three names are different points people mark on one excitation plot. IEEE C57.13.1-2017 clauses 6.5 and 12 tell you to compare the curve with the manufacturer's curve and to take readings near the knee. They do not define a 30-degree knee, a 45-degree knee, or a 10/50 knee. Say which marker you used.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.D.4; IEEE C57.13.1-2017, clauses 6.5 and 12

question: A potential-transformer check includes polarity. Valence’s PT/VT back-to-basics list, and ATS 7.10.2, both treat a wrong polarity as:
choices: Acceptable if the ratio is close
A failed test; the marks have to agree
Fixed by changing the fuse size
Only a metering problem, not a relay problem
explanation: Polarity has to match the marks. A reversed VT in a directional or synchronizing scheme is a wrong torque or a wrong close. Ratio alone does not catch it. Credit: Valence, potential transformer testing.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.2.D.2; Valence, Potential transformer testing

question: Valence’s PT/VT checklist calls out primary and secondary fuse sizes because:
choices: Any fuse that fits is fine
A wrong fuse can open on a normal burden or fail to clear a faulted secondary
Fuses set the turns ratio
Fuses replace the polarity test
explanation: The fuse has to match the VT and the burden. Too small and it opens in service; too large and a shorted secondary is not cleared. That check is visual against the drawings, then the ratio and polarity tests still happen. Credit: Valence.
reference: Valence, Potential transformer testing; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.2 includes fuse verification in the inspection

question: Turns ratio on a tapped VT, when the taps are accessible, is performed:
choices: On the in-service tap only
On all tap positions you can reach
Only if the fuse is blown
At DC
explanation: ATS 7.10.2 calls for a turns-ratio test on all tap positions. A bad tap will not show on the tap you happened to find in service. Valence’s list says the same thing.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.2.B.3; Valence, Potential transformer testing

question: A low-voltage turns-ratio check on a PT proves:
choices: The nameplate accuracy class at full voltage and full burden
That the ratio and polarity are in the right neighborhood for the marks, not the revenue accuracy
The fuse rating
Excitation knee at rated voltage
explanation: A handheld TTR applies a small voltage. It will catch a wrong tap or a reversed winding. It will not reproduce the factory accuracy test at 90, 100, and 110 percent voltage. ATS 7.10.2 still requires the ratio and the polarity check.
reference: Valence, Potential transformer testing; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.2

question: VT secondary burden is measured so you can see whether:
choices: The connected relays and cable exceed what the VT was rated to drive
The primary fuse is the right class
The oil is wet
The core ground is lifted
explanation: Burden is the load on the secondary. Too much and the VT sags and the relay or meter sees the wrong voltage. ATS 7.10.2 includes measuring the voltage-circuit burden at the transformer terminals and comparing it with the rating.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.2

question: ATS 7.10.1.B.1 insulation-resistance test on a current transformer and its secondary wiring is:
choices: 10 kV dc for 10 minutes
1000 V dc for one minute, unless solid-state parts cannot take that voltage
A power-factor test at 10 kV only
Optional for relaying CTs
explanation: Each CT and its secondary wiring is tested to ground at 1000 V dc for one minute. If solid-state parts cannot tolerate that, follow the manufacturer. The minimum resistance is Table 100.5, not a guess.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.1 and D.1

question: ATS 7.10.1.B.4 requires an excitation test:
choices: On every metering CT and never on a relaying CT
On current transformers used for relaying, in accordance with IEEE C57.13.1
Only if the ratio already failed
With the primary left connected to the bus
explanation: Relaying CTs get the excitation test. IEEE C57.13.1-2017 clause 6.5 compares the result with the manufacturer’s curve and uses it to find shorted turns. Clause 12 is how the test is run. Metering CTs still get ratio and polarity.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.4 and D.4; ref. IEEE C57.13.1-2017, clauses 6.5 and 12

question: ATS 7.1.1.A.7 says the current and voltage transformer ratios in switchgear must:
choices: Match the drawings
Be the highest ratio in the catalog
Be ignored if the relay is microprocessor
Match the cable shield resistance
explanation: A CT ratio that is not the ratio on the drawing makes every relay setting wrong in primary amperes. The check is visual against the nameplate and the drawing, before the electrical tests in 7.10.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.1.1.A.7

question: Instrument transformers mounted on a liquid-filled power transformer are tested by ATS 7.2.2.B.16:
choices: Under section 7.10
With the transformer turns-ratio set only
By oil power factor alone
Not at all, if the nameplate ratio is printed
explanation: Bushing CTs and other instrument transformers get the 7.10 tests: insulation resistance, polarity, ratio, and, for relaying CTs, excitation. The power-transformer ratio test does not cover them.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.B.16 and D.16

question: ATS 7.10.1 has you run an excitation test on relaying CTs. What does it confirm?
choices: Has the right ratio only
Matches its accuracy class and has no shorted turns, against the manufacturer’s curve
Is a metering CT
Needs no demagnetizing
explanation: Shorted turns and a wiring fault show up as a curve that is not the one the manufacturer drew. ATS 7.10.1.B.4 requires the test on relaying CTs and 7.10.1.D.4 compares it with that curve or with this guide.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.4 and D.4; ref. IEEE C57.13.1-2017, clause 6.5

question: How is the voltage method for a CT excitation test run?
choices: Applying AC to the secondary with the primary open, after demagnetizing
Applying DC to the primary while the secondary is shorted
Meggering the primary at 10 kV
Leaving the CT on the live bus
explanation: This is the usual field method because it does not need a high-current set. Clause 12.2.1 says to demagnetize first (see 5.1). The primary stays open. ATS 7.10.1.B.4 is the test that uses this method.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.4; ref. IEEE C57.13.1-2017, clauses 5.1 and 12.2.1

question: When can you run an in-service burden test on a CT circuit?
choices: The secondary is open
Secondary current is flowing, preferably near rated current
The primary is meggered
The CT is above the knee for 10 minutes
explanation: The test asks whether the CT can push a known current, set by its ratio, into a known burden and still hold its accuracy. ATS 7.10.1.B.5 measures that burden at the shorting block. An open secondary is not this test.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.5; ref. IEEE C57.13.1-2017, clause 6.7

question: On a dc (battery) polarity check of a CT with correct marks, the meter:
choices: Does not move
Kicks upscale when the battery is connected and downscale when it is opened
Kicks downscale on connection if X1 is positive
Reads the knee voltage
explanation: A small DC source is touched to the secondary and an analog meter watches the primary mark. Upscale on connect and downscale on release means the marks agree, for the hookup in that clause. ATS 7.10.1.D.2 fails the CT if the polarity does not match the marks. Clause 9 also allows AC and current methods.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.2 and D.2; ref. IEEE C57.13.1-2017, clause 9.1

question: For a CT excitation test, the ammeter should read rms. The voltmeter should be:
choices: Peak-reading only
Average-responding, scaled to match an rms meter on a sine wave
A DC millivoltmeter
A megohmmeter
explanation: The winding is nonlinear, so the voltage wave is not a clean sine. An average-responding meter, with bandwidth through the third harmonic, keeps the voltage reading from chasing those harmonics. ATS 7.10.1.D.4 still compares the curve you plot with the manufacturer’s curve.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.D.4; ref. IEEE C57.13.1-2017, clause 12.2

question: Plotting a CT excitation curve, which readings matter most?
choices: Only the origin
The readings near the knee
Only the current at 1 V
The DC resistance
explanation: The knee is where the curve leaves the straight part. A plot that stops early cannot be compared with the manufacturer’s curve. Clause 6.5 is why ATS 7.10.1 asks for that comparison on a relaying CT.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.D.4; ref. IEEE C57.13.1-2017, clause 12.2.1

question: What does a dc resistance measurement on a CT secondary help you find?
choices: The insulation power factor
A high-resistance joint in the winding or the connected wiring
The knee voltage
Polarity
explanation: The resistance should match the specification, and the test is also looking for a bad connection. It is not the excitation test and it is not polarity. ATS 7.10.1 still requires the ratio, polarity, and, for relaying CTs, the excitation test in the same guide.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1; ref. IEEE C57.13.1-2017, clause 6.4

question: A bar-type CT, as ATS 7.10.1 uses the term, has:
choices: No primary of its own; only a window
A primary bar that is part of the transformer
A split core that opens after the cable is made up
A secondary that is never grounded
explanation: The section tests the primary of a bar-type CT with the secondary grounded. The bar is the primary. A window CT has to have the cable pass through the opening, so it is placed before that cable is terminated. ATS does not give a separate procedure named split-core.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.6

question: The temperature-rise rating of a CT is taken from:
choices: Table 100.18
The CT nameplate, checked against the drawings
The relay tap
A 10 A microhmmeter
explanation: ATS 7.10.1 starts by comparing the nameplate with the drawings. That is where the ratings, including temperature rise, are read. Table 100.18, the relay tap, and a microhmmeter do not set that rating.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.A.1

question: A CT that can be opened and placed around a cable that is already terminated is commonly called:
choices: Bar-type
Split-core
A network protector
A watts-loss arrester
explanation: A split-core CT opens on a hinge or joint so it can go around a conductor that is already terminated. A solid window CT needs that conductor threaded through the opening before the termination is made. ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.6 and B.7 name bar-type CTs for the primary insulation-resistance and withstand tests. They do not define the split-core name, and they do not tell you the cable must pass through a window as a contrast with a bar-type unit.
reference: Engineering fundamentals (split-core CT); ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.6 and B.7

question: A bar-type CT on a 15 kV, 95 kV BIL system gets the optional acceptance dielectric withstand on its primary. With no other data, the ac test voltage is:
choices: 34 kV
36 kV
explanation: ATS has the bar-type CT primary withstand run at the Table 100.9 value, which for 15 kV nominal, 95 kV BIL is 25.5 kV ac. That table comes from the instrument-transformer standard's field-test guidance. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.7 and Table 100.9; IEEE C57.13-2016, 8.5.2.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.7 and Table 100.9; ref. IEEE C57.13-2016, 8.5.2

question: Why are instrument-transformer field withstand voltages set well below the factory test values, and lower again for periodic tests?
choices: Field sets cannot reach factory voltage
Repeated dielectric tests stress the insulation; initial field tests are kept to about 75% of the factory value and periodic tests to about 65%
Field tests are dc, so they read higher
Factory values include a 2:1 safety margin that is removed in the field
explanation: The instrument-transformer standard warns that dielectric tests are severe and can hasten breakdown. It recommends initial user tests no higher than 75% of factory test voltage, and periodic tests no higher than 65%. ATS Table 100.9 notes that its field values come from this clause. Source: IEEE C57.13-2016, 8.5.2.
reference: IEEE C57.13-2016, 8.5.2; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.9

question: ATS has you compare the measured CT circuit burden to the CT rating. A relaying CT is rated C200, and the measured secondary circuit burden is 1.4 Ω. That burden is:
choices: Within the rating, since a C200 CT is rated for the 2.0 Ω standard burden
Too high, since C200 means a 0.2 Ω limit
Too high, since 1.4 Ω exceeds 1.0 Ω
Not comparable to a C rating
explanation: A C200 rating means the CT will deliver 200 V at 20 times rated current (100 A) into the standard burden that matches it, B-2.0, which is 2.0 Ω, with no more than 10% ratio error. A 1.4 Ω circuit is below that. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.5 and D.5; IEEE C57.13-2016, 6.4.1.3 and Table 13.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.D.5; ref. IEEE C57.13-2016, 6.4.1.3 and Table 13

question: ATS says CT ratio errors must meet the instrument-transformer standard. For a C- or T-class relaying CT at rated current, the ratio error limit is:
explanation: Relaying CTs in C and T classes are held to 3% ratio error at rated current and 10% at 20 times rated current. (Small window CTs with few turns may exceed 3% at rated current.) The 0.3% figure is a metering class. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.D.3; IEEE C57.13-2016, Table 12.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.D.3; ref. IEEE C57.13-2016, 6.4 and Table 12

question: A 0.3-class metering CT is ratio tested at 100% of rated current. The ratio correction factor must fall within:
explanation: For accuracy class 0.3 at 100% rated current, the correction factor limits are 0.9970 to 1.0030, which is ±0.3%. At 10% current the band doubles to 0.9940 to 1.0060. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.D.3; IEEE C57.13-2016, 5.3 and Table 8.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.D.3; ref. IEEE C57.13-2016, 5.3 and Table 8

question: A multi-ratio relaying CT is nameplated C400 at 2000:5. You connect it at the 1000:5 tap. Per IEEE C57.13-2016:
choices: C400 still applies at every tap
The relay accuracy class applies only to the full winding unless stated otherwise, so the tap's capability is lower
The tap doubles the class to C800
Taps are not allowed on C-class CTs
explanation: The relay class applies to the full winding unless otherwise specified. On a C-class CT, tapped sections must be arranged so the ratio can be calculated. So don't assume C400 at a tap; check the manufacturer's tap data or the excitation curve for that tap. Source: IEEE C57.13-2016, 6.4.2.

question: A CT has a 1 A secondary and a C100 rating. Per IEEE C57.13-2016, what burden matches that rating?
choices: 1 Ω
5 Ω
explanation: For secondaries other than 5 A, the equivalent burden is the terminal voltage ÷ (IS × 20). 100 V ÷ (1 A × 20) = 5 Ω. Source: IEEE C57.13-2016, Table 13 note a.
reference: IEEE C57.13-2016, Table 13 note a

question: What does a field CT ratio test, as IEEE C57.13.1 describes it, prove?
choices: The CT meets its 0.3 metering accuracy
The CT won't saturate on any fault
The installed ratio and tap wiring are what was specified; it doesn't prove accuracy class
The burden is within rating
explanation: C57.13.1 says the ratio test verifies the stated ratio, and that taps are correct and wired to the right terminals. It is not an accuracy test. Excitation and burden checks answer other questions. Source: IEEE C57.13.1-2017, 6.1; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.3.

question: Why does CT polarity matter so much in differential and directional schemes?
choices: Polarity only matters for metering CTs
A reversed CT reads zero current
Those relays compare or sum currents, so a reversed CT makes normal load look like a fault (or hides a real one)
Polarity changes the CT ratio
explanation: Polarity proves secondary current flows the predicted direction for a given primary direction. That is essential wherever currents are summed, compared differentially, or compared with voltages in a relay. Source: IEEE C57.13.1-2017, 6.2; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.D.2.

question: During a dc battery polarity check on a CT, what does IEEE C57.13.1 warn about when you break the battery connection?
choices: A dangerous voltage can appear; parallel a resistor across the winding first or use a hot stick or rubber gloves
The battery can explode from back-feed
The CT ratio changes permanently
Nothing, since 9 V can't create a hazard
explanation: Interrupting the dc in an inductive winding can generate a dangerous voltage spike. The guide suggests a resistor near the winding's dc resistance placed in parallel before disconnecting, or connecting and disconnecting with a hot stick or rubber gloves. Source: IEEE C57.13.1-2017, 9.1 (warning).
reference: IEEE C57.13.1-2017, 9.1 (warning)

question: How does IEEE C57.13.1 describe demagnetizing a CT with a variable ac voltage?
choices: Apply dc to the primary and switch it off quickly
Short the secondary for one minute
Reverse the battery leads on a polarity test
Apply ac to the secondary high enough to saturate the core, then reduce it slowly and continuously to zero
explanation: The voltage method drives the core above saturation and then ramps the voltage smoothly down to zero, using the same hookup as the excitation test. Demagnetize after any dc test, since dc leaves remanence. Source: IEEE C57.13.1-2017, 5.1 and 9.1 (caution).
reference: IEEE C57.13.1-2017, 5.1 and 9.1 (caution)

question: Why should a CT never be operated with its secondary open while primary current can flow?
choices: The CT ratio doubles
Hazardous peak voltages can develop across the open secondary
The primary current stops flowing
The relay sees reversed polarity
explanation: IEEE C57.13 says CTs should never run with the secondary open because hazardous peak voltages may result. Short the secondary at the shorting block before lifting any wire. Source: IEEE C57.13-2016, 6.7.1.

question: IEEE C57.13 says a conforming CT can survive an open secondary for 1 minute at rated current times rating factor, provided the open-circuit voltage doesn't exceed what?
choices: 600 V rms
3500 V peak; above that, consider a varistor or spark gap across the secondary
120 V rms
10 kV peak with no protection needed
explanation: The standard's emergency capability is one minute open-circuited if the open-circuit voltage stays at or below 3500 V peak. For CTs that can exceed it, the user should consider a voltage-limiting device. That is a survival rating, not permission to open a live secondary. Source: IEEE C57.13-2016, 6.7.1.

question: With the primary still energized but carrying no load, a tech plans to lift the CT secondary ground. IEEE C57.13.1 warns that:
choices: It's safe because no current is flowing
Only the relay will be damaged
The CT will demagnetize itself
Dangerous voltage can appear on the secondary through electrostatic coupling even with no primary current
explanation: The guide's warning: removing the secondary ground without de-energizing the primary can put dangerous voltage on the secondary circuit by electrostatic coupling, even with zero primary current. Source: IEEE C57.13.1-2017, Annex A.1 (warning).
reference: IEEE C57.13.1-2017, Annex A.1 (warning)

question: CT excitation tests are normally run by applying voltage to the secondary with the primary open. Why not drive it from the primary?
choices: Primary drive would put high voltage on the open secondary and needs a very large test current
The primary has no magnetizing path
It would reverse the polarity marks
Primary drive can't reach the knee
explanation: Theoretically the primary is where magnetizing flux originates. In practice primary excitation creates high voltage at the open secondary terminals and needs a high test current, so the secondary voltage method is used except in special cases. Source: IEEE C57.13.1-2017, 12.3 (caution on primary excitation); ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.4.
reference: IEEE C57.13.1-2017, 12.3 (caution on primary excitation); ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.4

question: You apply excitation voltage across one tap section of a multi-ratio CT. What happens across the full winding?
choices: Nothing appears on the untested sections
The full winding sees exactly the same voltage
A proportionally higher voltage appears across the whole winding by autotransformer action
The untested sections short out
explanation: C57.13.1 warns that voltage applied to part of the secondary induces a proportional voltage across the full winding. Keep clear of all terminals and don't hold voltage above the knee longer than the readings need. Source: IEEE C57.13.1-2017, 12.1.

question: A C100 relaying CT with a 5 A secondary feeds a total loop burden of 1.5 Ω. At 20 times rated current (100 A secondary), roughly what voltage would the CT need to produce?
choices: 7.5 V, well within rating
100 V, exactly at its rating
150 V, more than the C100 rating, so it is likely to saturate
30 V, within rating
explanation: V = I × Z = 100 A × 1.5 Ω = 150 V. A C100 rating means the CT delivers 100 V to a standard burden at 20 times rated current within the 10% error limit. Asking for 150 V pushes it past the knee. Source: IEEE C57.13-2016, 6.4.1.3 and Table 13.
